query: Which method can be used for reduce the sintering temperature, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using spark plasma sintering (SPS) reduces the sintering temperature needed for fabricating refractory high‐entropy alloys because its rapid heating and applied pressure enhance densification at lower temperatures compared to conventional sintering methods.
generation.material_initial_state: Mechanically alloyed refractory HEA powders with fine, homogeneous microstructure
generation.intervention: Processing the alloy powders using spark plasma sintering (SPS) instead of conventional high-temperature sintering
generation.conditions: An inert atmosphere, application of moderate pressure combined with pulsed electric currents, and reduced sintering temperatures (e.g., around 1200°C)
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced diffusion kinetics at particle contacts and localized Joule heating that promotes neck formation
generation.mechanism: The coupling of applied pressure with pulsed electric currents in SPS accelerates atomic diffusion and particle bonding, thereby lowering the activation energy required for full densification while minimizing grain growth
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy will achieve high-density consolidation with a refined microstructure at lower sintering temperatures than those required by conventional furnace sintering
generation.baseline: Conventional sintering methods typically require higher temperatures (e.g., >1400°C) to achieve similar densification and phase formation
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the temperature reduction may depend on powder particle size, mixing homogeneity, and the specific SPS parameters used
generation.uncertainty: While SPS is expected to reduce the sintering temperature, the precise degree of reduction and its impact on long-term mechanical properties may vary among different refractory HEA systems

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical mechanically alloyed refractory HEA powders. Sinter one set using conventional high-temperature sintering (e.g., >1400°C) and the other set using SPS at a reduced temperature (e.g., ~1200°C) under the same atmospheric and pressure conditions. Compare the density, microstructural homogeneity, and phase constitution of the sintered samples.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM for grain size and porosity assessment)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SPS-processed samples do not achieve comparable densification and phase purity at the lower sintering temperature, or if they exhibit inferior microstructural or mechanical properties relative to those produced by conventional sintering, then the hypothesis that SPS reduces required sintering temperature would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: According to the traditional alloy design theory, ordered phases or intermetallic compounds will form as the number of alloying elements increases. However, Yeh et al. observes that simple solid solution phases, instead of intermetallic compounds, are formed in an equiatomic quinary alloy. Subsequently, they propose a new alloy system, termed high entropy alloys (HEAs), which contain at least five principal elements, each having the atomic percentage between 5% and 35% [ [1] , [2] ]. Since the development of HEAs, a substantial number of studies on HEA have been performed. Some of these studies are focused on alloys comprised of elements with low melting points, such as AlCoCrCuFeNi system alloys [ [3] , [4] ], commonly exhibiting high ductility and low strength. On the other hand, refractory HEAs have exhibited advantages of high yield strength at room and elevated temperature. The requirements for designing novel metallic alloys that are capable of surpassing a whole set of specific properties of currently available commercial alloys are, at present, a subject of high demand in the industry. For instance, an improved combination of metallic alloys should possess strength and ductility while maintaining a relatively low cost. This is especially true when one is dealing with materials for high-temperature applications. Therefore, new engineering solutions are needed for novel materials that outperform the capabilities of the currently used Ni-based alloys. One of the prospective innovative materials that could be able to meet the requirements of such demanding applications, especially in the aviation and aerospace industries, may be refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). These are also known by other names, such as complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). These materials have been extensively studied in recent years [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] due to their very interesting combination of properties in some of the compositions.
